utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we hear the evidence of the next witness, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling. The Chamber refers to Krstic's request for reconsideration of the order dated 13th of March, 2013, filed confidentially on the 19th of March, 2013, in which counsel for Mr. Krstic requests reconsideration of the Chamber's oral ruling of 13th of March, 2013, in which Mr. Krstic was ordered to testify in this case on 25th of March, 2013, on the basis that the relevant medical report did not identify medical reasons which would amount to good cause for Mr. Krstic not to comply with the terms of subpoena dated 23rd of October, 2012. Mr. Krstic requests that this order be set aside on the basis that, number one, he was not given an opportunity to make submissions as to the meaning and impact of the medical report; and number two, that the Chamber's oral ruling appeared to be inconsistent with the medical report. The Chamber was put on notice of the health concerns referred to by Mr. Krstic when he refused to testify in this case on the 7th of February, 2013, which prompted the Chamber to order the preparation of a more detailed medical report evaluating whether Mr. Krstic was fit to testify and assessing the possible impact of testifying in this case on his health. In deciding to order that Mr. Krstic testify in this case, the Chamber was not incognizant that doing so could cause considerable distress to Mr. Krstic, but concluded on balance that any potential impact on his health as identified in the medical report was not sufficiently serious to amount to good cause not to comply with the terms of subpoena. The Chamber finds that the test for reconsideration of its oral ruling has not been met, given the failure to demonstrate there was a clear error of reasoning or that reconsideration was necessary in order to prevent injustice. The Registry is instructed to communicate this ruling to Mr. Krstic and his legal representatives. That said, shall we bring in the next witness? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could just raise one quick housekeeping matter, Mr. President, and this refers to something that I think Mr. Robinson alluded to in a recent submission, it may be obvious to everyone in the courtroom but I was simply seeking confirmation, and that is that with respect to Mr. Martic, irrespective of anything else that may happen in the upcoming days, that we get official confirmation of what, as I said, now seems obvious, and that is that the Prosecution will not be cross-examining him next week at least for our -- for purposes of our scheduling and preparation and allocation of resources. So I -- that may be obviated by the Court's response to Mr. Robinson's request in respect of the current appearance date. But one way or another, I think it's clear that the cross-examination cannot proceed next week. And we'd just like the reassurance of a confirmation of what does seem obvious to us from the Court so that we don't engage in unnecessary and wasteful efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of the situation and is considering the matter, and I think the Chamber will come back to that issue during the course of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add that we had filed our submission on that issue concerning the assignment of counsel before Mr. Tieger had made an oral representation which included a suggestion that the Chamber may not have jurisdiction over that issue, and I imagine the Chamber is well aware of two decisions which give the Trial Chamber jurisdiction over that issue, one of them being in the Popovic case, which you participated; the other being in the Mico Stanisic case. So I could supply those to your Chamber if you're interested; otherwise, I just wanted to make you aware of that so that we didn't waste time bouncing the issue back to the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the decision in the Popovic case about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was the decision on the third request for review of the Registry decision on the assignment of co-counsel for Radivoje Miletic on the 20th of February, 2007, where the Trial Chamber reversed the Registrar's decision that attorney Nenad Petrusic could not be co-counsel for Mr. Miletic because he didn't speak English. And in the Mico Stanisic case there was a decision on the review of the Registrar's decision concerning co-counsel for Mico Stanisic on the 24th of April, 2007, where the Trial Chamber found that it did have jurisdiction to review the Registrar's denial of assignment of co-counsel for Mico Stanisic on the grounds that he didn't speak English but upheld the Registrar's decision in that instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that both of those decisions related to the accused or one of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll bring in the next witness. Next witness is Sosic, to be sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sosic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Sosic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I have given several statements. I don't know which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you recently read and signed one of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very recently your associates came to my hotel. I read the entire statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please be mindful of pauses before question and answer. Please look at the transcript and watch the cursor. We should speak slowly and make a pause between what I say and what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I call up 1D7941 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you see before you the statement you've given?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: If only we could make this larger because it's very tiny now. Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the statement I've read and seen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the Serbian version on one side and show the last page to identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect your words? Is everything correct? Is there a need to correct something?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: As far as I could see, everything is well interpreted. Like all the witnesses, one could always add something, but that is the gist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today as you were asked during the interview, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this package under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the package includes three associated exhibits. None of them appeared on our Rule 65 ter list and I would ask that they be added because we didn't have them at the time that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having briefly looked at the witness statements which refers to those three items, the Chamber is not satisfied that they form indispensable and inseparable part of the statement as well as their relevance. So the Chamber is not minded to admit them at the moment. Good morning, Ms. Iodice. Do you have any objection to the admission of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: To the admission of the statement, no, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 1D7941 will be Exhibit D3138 [Realtime transcript read in error "D3938"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I right in assuming that I can lead some of the documents live?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Karadzic, but it's a separate matter whether Chamber will admit them having been satisfied with their relevance and probative value.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Professor Mirko Sosic's statement in English. [In English] Professor Dr. Mirko Sosic worked as a professor at the University Clinic Centre, the Clinic for Thoracic Surgery. He was and is a member of the Academy of Sciences and Arts and professor and prominent surgeon. From August 1992 when he left Sarajevo, he worked at the Koran hospital at Pale. Mirko Sosic considers that Muslims and Serbian communists started putting pressure on Serbian staff in the 1960s which resulted in many professionals leaving Sarajevo. However, from the moment the political parties were formed the doctors were divided on ethnicity. Professor Sosic first saw members of the Muslim paramilitary in March 1992 when the forces practically occupied Kosevo university hospital. Following this occupation, the suspicion and hostility towards the Serbs increased both towards the employees and the patients. After the first clashes broke out in Sarajevo, a Crisis Staff was formed in the university clinic, and from the moment Serbian doctors were cleared out of all positions. On April the 4th, 1992, Professor Sosic attempted to travel from Pale to Sarajevo. He came across a large group of people who had been stopped by armed Muslims on the Pale-Sarajevo bus line and were ordered to go back to where they had come from. Mirko Sosic was only able to return to Sarajevo a few days later on the civilian -- last civilian flight. At this point an internal blockade placed on the city. Guards were organised by the tenants of residential buildings with entrance and exit of the buildings being strictly controlled. The people who checked this were armed paramilitary groups who would enter apartments they considered suspicious, search and then ransack them. From the first few days of the clashes in Sarajevo, there was an internal blockade in Sarajevo. Guards organised by the tenants of residential buildings strictly called entry and exit from the building. On June 1992, he saw trucks travelling down the road and heard two shots fired. As the truck passed, he saw that it had a weapon mounted on its body and projectiles were being fired from the weapon; however, this Muslim neighbours denied -- his Muslim neighbours denied this. Other weapons were placed around the city. A cannon was placed in the underground entrance of the emergency room at the hospital. The cannon would be pulled out, fire two or three projectiles, and then be returned. Professor Mirko Sosic joined the Koran war hospital in Pale, and as far as he is aware, Serbian doctors respected in full the medical code of honour and ethics, making no difference between patients on any basis whatsoever. All staff at the hospital showed significant attention to wounded victims of all nationalities. Captured UNPROFOR soldiers were kept in good psychological and physical state. Throughout his time in Sarajevo, Professor Mirko Sosic was informed that many Serbs died in the hospital for lack of medical aid. Several times, according to Professor Sosic's knowledge of events and information from fellow doctors, the Muslims opened artillery fire from the hospital -- Kosevo hospital area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Professor, to tell us about a few documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 1D10031 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the circumstances of the captured UN soldiers and how?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. One day - and I can't give you the exact date but I see here that it's displayed - I was informed by the then-health minister Dragan Kalinic that I was put in charge of visiting the captured UN soldiers who were in a nearby camp to see the status of their health, what they need, and their situation, in order to inform the ministry to see what they wished, what they needed in terms of medicine, what state of mind they were in, et cetera. I accepted, and because I wanted to be accommodating to those people, supposing that they must be fearful, I contacted a colleague at the ministry who is an excellent doctor and who spoke English, and another woman who was a volunteer and worked in a hospital, she was Dutch, a retired pharmacist --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's already in your statement. Could you just tell us what this letter is in the chain of events concerning these examinations. What is the letter on page 1? Is this the request?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's this gentleman, the major, writing to Colonel Batinic, expressing their wish to help, that somebody should provide care for the health of those captured people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you publish this anywhere? Is this in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: No. From memory I made some notes, it's a manuscript, but it's never been published anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you help us, because we don't have the translation yet, what is the second part of the text?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we zoom in a little more. Yes, the second part. It's part of my report, where I say that we were invited by the captain to look in on the eight captured members of the UNPROFOR, and that's my description of their accommodation, their location, their treatment, their physical and mental status, an examination by a team of doctors to establish which of them are the most vulnerable, to put it that way, et cetera. I suggested that, first of all, we should decide how to talk to them because I was a civilian, I was a doctor, just visiting. I wanted to see how we are going to conduct these interviews. There were two suggestions: To talk to them as a group or to talk to them individually. Everybody said they wanted it to be individual. So we set aside one whole afternoon and talked to each one of them individually. Each of them had their own story, their own view of the situation. At first they looked fearful, but when they realised that we were well-intentioned, especially when they saw that lady who was able to speak to a Dutch officer in his own language, the atmosphere that began as tense turned gradually into a friendly one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see who signed this report. Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is my signature and the signature of my colleague who went with me, that was Mr. Babic who was a urologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you see your signature, Doctor, now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see a signature here. It just says signed by Professor Dr. Mirko Sosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this an authentic text?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is here on the following page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: This is the list of the prisoners or whatever we might call them, the persons who were members of the UNPROFOR and who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this to be admitted as an MFI document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Iodice, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3139, Your Honours. I just correct the record, the 92 ter statement is Exhibit D3138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Sosic, you said that doctors of Serbian ethnicity were removed from various positions. What happened with these Serbian doctors later on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, the attitude, perhaps it would be good to illustrate it with several examples. In the beginning of the war I was head of clinic. That was my duty. And at one of the meetings held for all heads of clinics, which was organised by the Crisis Staff presided by my colleague Professor Dr. Faruk Konjhodzic, when I came to attend the meeting, the first thing he asked me was what I was doing there, that that was no place for me, and I still held the position as head of clinic. And I considered that as a sort of inofficial replacement. And then when I returned to the clinic I learned from one of my younger colleagues who used to be my assistant, that he was informed that he was to take over the duty as the head of the clinic. So he told me privately, "Well, you see, I didn't want to tell you this. This should be among ourselves. We would keep the same relations between us. When we do the rounds, you will lead the rounds. We will determine who needs to be operated so that we would not make a big fuss of all that." And, you know, one feels rather uncomfortable when, after 25 or 30 years of employment and socialising with colleagues whom I knew since my high school days and who I believed I was on good terms with, suddenly you feel something like this, that they take this sort of attitude towards you. But then when I discussed this with other colleagues, I saw that it was not directed against me but that the others were treated in the same way. Another colleague of mine who was the head of the traumatology clinic at the time, which was overwhelmed with the wounded at the time because the war began and the war always entails trauma, Professor Jovo Vranic, he told me, "Well, you faired quite well." And why did I fair well? I was told publicly by the head of -- and he said, "Do not ever dare to address me," even though he was the head of the clinic and he was supposed to write reports about the situation in the clinic. So these were just some illustrations of the situation. And on a daily basis we witnessed that someone went missing without a trace. One doctor or another doctor, they were no longer there. Or this one was detained, another tried to commit suicide, another one was wounded and so on. On the first day of the war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On the 4th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can just ask you to slow down a little bit so that everything would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that from the first day of the conflict, when the conflict broke out, that is to say, the 4th of April, a murder was attempted of the dean of the faculty of medicine. That was Professor Dr. Borisa Starovic. It was only thanks to the fact that he bowed down at the moment when he was entering his car and therefore the bullet hit him on his shoulder blade and his back rather than hit him in the head when he was getting into the car. Another family of my colleague, his wife and daughter were wounded while they were sitting in their kitchen. So regularly it happened that doctors were the victims I might freely say of assassinations. A well-known incident was the murder of retired head Dr. Professor Vojko Sorbat. And then Professor Mijatovic, who was returning home from work, when he tried to cross the bridge over the Vrbanja was wounded by a sniper and he hardly survived. It was a very serious injury and he had to be operated on 11 times in order to reconstruct his alimentary tract because the injuries were very serious. And let me not speak any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Sosic, yes, I'm very sorry to interrupt you, but our time is rather limited. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a Crisis Staff which was making those decisions. Can you just tell us briefly what that was about, what Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: As I understood, that was organised ad hoc, a body that was established ad hoc, and it replaced all other administrative organs of the clinical centre and the hospital. They had the authority not just to control everything in the organisational sense of the word but also in the medical one. They controlled everything, organised everything, and also oversaw all the activities in the hospital, including all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the basis of such attitude towards you and your other colleagues of Serb ethnicity? Were you politically engaged or politically active in any political party at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: If I may venture to comment, I was never a member of any political party. I liked surgery and I held a prominent position as the president of the surgical association of all of Yugoslavia. So that was my preoccupation. And as a student and as a successful sportsman, I was a member of the communist party. They just enrolled me into the party, but later on I was not active at all so I was probably thrown out of the party. And after that I was never a member of any party at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You went back and after the beginning of the war in Sarajevo what was your intention? Why did you want to return to Sarajevo? Did you intend to stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Of course. I'm a native of Sarajevo. Everything I had, everything I had achieved was connected with this Sarajevo. My childhood, my career, my friendships, everything was in Sarajevo. In 1986 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996."] I received the award of the city of Sarajevo for achievements in the medical profession, which was the greatest acknowledgement awarded by the city of Sarajevo. Of course, I was just one of the team members who were awarded. And in addition to that, it was also my conviction that there should be no war and that conflicts can be resolved peacefully. And lastly, I had the responsibility, I was head of the clinic and I had the responsibility to the patients and my colleagues and myself and my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 15 it should be 1986. Professor, did you record or review later on at any point and make a list of doctors who, like you, had to leave Sarajevo eventually?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may, if I may tell you this first. The attitude which was partial towards the Serbs and I began to notice that from day-to-day. And then later on I remembered a thought which was very clever and it wasn't mine. You see, I didn't feel myself a Serb or a nationalist or anything. I considered myself a member of my family and a surgeon and an internationalist. And I found a sentence which said if they insult you and attack you as a Jew, you have to defend yourself as a Jew. That is to say, by analogy, if they attack you and insult you as a Serb, you have to defend yourself as a Serb. I think that Mrs. Hannah Arendt, a prominent philosopher, said this. And I found this to be a logical explanation in a way because you are simply forced to go where you are being pushed, because otherwise you don't belong anywhere. And looking around and looking at my colleagues, I could not stop wondering how those people were going missing or were leaving. And then in an amateur way, I began to compile a list of people I knew who had been prominent doctors. I stuck to the medical profession only, and these were the people who were leaving Sarajevo that I entered in my amateur's list. The list included around 450 doctors, you see, and I guarantee that 95 per cent of those doctors did not belong to any political party. 70 or 80 per cent of them were prominent, well-respected professors at the university, doctors, and so on. What I found strange about this - and I could not that then nor could I discover it now - what was the reason to create such conditions that would force these people to leave Sarajevo. Wasn't it detrimental for the city and the social environment and the profession when one populated place loses 450 doctors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D10029 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this to appear on the screen, Doctor, when you mentioned the assassinations, can you tell us about the Serbian lines. How far were they from the places where these people lost their lives? Were the Serbs able to fire from there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can assess - and I'm a native of Sarajevo and I liked to walk the surrounding mountains, especially Trebevic - in my assessment, it was 3 or 4 kilometres as the crow flies or perhaps even a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can we see on the screen now, Professor? Is this your list?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I initiated this, but you know how it is. I showed this list to some of my colleagues and then they criticised me and said, "Well, how could you have forgotten this man?" And so the list was expanded. So I couldn't claim I knew everything because they would tell me, "Why didn't you include this man? He went there," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it is a collective work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, made by friends.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you assist us how this is relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have this feeling for justice, and as for law, Mr. Robinson can judge about that. We are showing what happened in various places with the Serbs and Muslims. We are listening how the wild Serbs attacked Sarajevo which was a peaceful town; however, Sarajevo was militarised and it was brutal towards the Serbs. And the list of 400-odd doctors who fled and were not members of the SDS and were not political activists just fills this picture, so this is the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Iodice, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to note that the Prosecution filed a motion to exclude the evidence of this witness and the evidence related to this document was included in paragraph 16 of the old statement, and in the response the accused agreed to remove this exhibit from the -- from Dr. Sosic's statement once it was finalised. So that's the first point. Second point is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Was the motion ruled upon by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, because once the accused agreed with the objections of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber asked us and we thought that the matter was closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And the second point is that the evidence contained about the doctors leaving Sarajevo that is now in the statement should be sufficient. There is no -- I don't see any value being added by this exhibit being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may respond. First of all, it corroborates the statement because these are specific people. And in addition to that, D130 to 133 are parts of a video-clip which have been admitted and they relate to this topic and the professor is featured in this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may add just one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: As to corroboration, it's -- the witness is stating -- it's the same source. So the relevance of the corroboration is limited. There is not an independent confirmation of the doctors that left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While I had some doubts, I allowed you to put those questions to Dr. Sosic and his evidence in the transcript. I think that's more than sufficient. The Chamber is not satisfied with the relevance of this document and we'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, you mentioned the late Professor Jovo Vranic, who was well respected and you said that you exchanged information with him. Can you tell us what was the most striking of all the things that Professor Vranic told you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, we were colleagues. We were born the same year, we held the same position, we happened to be in the same situation in the same kind of trouble and so on and so forth, so it was logical that during the war and after the war we talked and we co-operated. Professor Jovo Vranic wrote his memoirs of the war and he asked me to review them, to review that document of his that unfortunately had not been published, because in the meantime he passed away. However, at the time when I wanted to write that review I consulted with him. So I received explanations about his situation and about his impressions, about his memory of what happened during the war because, I repeat, he was the head of the traumatology clinic where most of the patients were, by the very nature of things, surgery. He confirmed to me what I knew, and it wasn't only me, we all knew that before the war broke out, already in the month of March, the hospital had been occupied by paramilitary organisations, and that all doctors, all of the officially employed doctors, had to be subjected to rigorous checks when entering the hospital that was quite informal. We were searched, frisked, we needed to open our bags and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have part of that book here, but I doubt that the Trial Chamber will need that. I'd like to ask you about another document, though. Can you tell us, as for health infrastructure, what did the Serbs manage to keep once they were expelled from town? What did you encounter? What did you have to do in terms of protecting the health of the population and of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: You know, at first glance this was a problem that could not be solved because in those parts of town that were under the control of the Serbs, there were a few health institutions that were not equipped for providing full medical care. The only hospital that was official that was in Kasindol was a pavilion-type hospital and it specialised in treating tuberculosis and chronic chest diseases. So without an operating room -- it was founded in 1921 and it certainly could not serve that basic purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what I have in mind here is 1D10025. So, Excellencies, I would be interested in the following. Does the Chamber accept this document? There's a translation too which shows the difficulties that Serb doctors encountered when expelled from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I ruled that it does not form part of -- indispensable and inseparable part of this witness's statement. As such, we did not admit it. As to be satisfied with the relevance or probative value, we have to see the documents, but I doubt whether -- if it has any much probative value. It's up to you to proceed or not, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering the document, but if your ruling is not to have it admitted, then I would like to ask for 1D10027, that is to say, the knowledge that Professor Sosic gained from Professor Vranic. It's pages 4 to 10 in e-court. That's what's been translated and I think that those six pages are sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, to save time, I'll tell you that the Chamber is not minded to admit either of the documents. In the future please ask Mr. Robinson how to proceed in tendering documents. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Excellencies. I have to say that I give Mr. Robinson top grades, but my personal feelings are primarily those of justice, not law, so that is why I say what I say. Thank you. At this point in time, I have no further questions for Professor Sosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Sosic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, that is, through your written statement instead of your oral testimony. And now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Iodice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Sosic. Doctor, you said today that you never joined any party, any political party; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, except I already mentioned this by way of a correction, that as a university student because of sports I was admitted into the communist party. But no, never, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also said in your statement that you were appointed minister of health during the time of Klickovic's government.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I would like to call 65 ter 24737. While we wait this is a newspaper article from "Knina" which is dated the 2nd of December, 1996, and it's about the -- and it is about the people who were appointed as members of the government of Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have hard copies for the -- for the witness if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note it's coming. We are still having technical difficulties uploading -- not coming. Yes. Shall we use ELMO. We are using Sanction now?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes. And if we can go to the third page in B/C/S and 5 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Dr. Sosic, you can see at the top of this page your name, Dr. Mirko Sosic. And at the end, the last sentence you can read: "... and he's a member of the Serbian Democratic Party." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have proper B/C/S page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor confirmed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So you were a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So you were a member of the SDS, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the custom is here. I was never a member of the SDS and, because of that, I had a bit of a problem to be appointed minister in the government. Now, the then-minister of health who put me up as a candidate, because before that I worked in a group of experts for the strategy of developing the health system, he said that it didn't matter, that it wasn't relevant at all, that he had carried out consultations on that, whether I was a member of the SDS or not, but I was never a member. This is here either on the basis of inertia or it's malicious or maybe people thought everybody had to be that. I was the only one who didn't really want to. How do I put this? I was aware of my own value and that as a surgeon and an expert I didn't have to be a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you mentioned a medal that you received in 1996. Did you also receive a medal in 1995? You were awarded with a medal by -- directly by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know the date. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't really matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: But do you remember that the person who awarded you that medal was Mr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Maybe if the witness could be provided with a copy. I also have in hard copy if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So if you could go to paragraph 7 of your statement, you talk about house searches. And when we met two days ago, you confirmed that nothing was stolen from your apartment; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when in your statement you have discussed all the weapons that you saw and the shelling you witnessed, you refer to the time that you were in Sarajevo up until mid-August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. I remember it was summertime, early in the morning, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 8 of your statement, you discuss the event where you witnessed a truck with a weapon mounted on its back. Do I understand your evidence correctly that you only heard two shots and then you saw a truck driving by with a weapon at its back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Partly. You know, I was in front of the door. It was 6.00 in the morning, summertime, and actually came to stand in for my wife because I could not be on this guard duty because of my duty at hospital. But then I heard shooting from the student dormitories in Bjelave. Now, was it two or three or whatever shots, but we heard these shots getting close to us slowly as it passed by my house. It wasn't a big truck. It was a small TAM truck and there was a weapon mounted on it. And as it passed by, then the shooting became more distant too. Now, was it two or three, but I could follow how it was moving on the basis of that sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And all I wanted to know whether you first heard a shot -- the shots and then you saw the truck driving by?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You did not see the truck shooting as it was driving by; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: You mean that moment of firing?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 9 you discuss a cannon that you saw in the vicinity of the emergency room in the hospital. Is it correct that you saw the cannon but you did not see the cannon firing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to correct you. This is the clinic of traumatology. It's not the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Secondly, invariably a siren would go off. And then -- you know, all of us in the hospital knew that, this was a warning for no one to go out. And then --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Dr. Sosic, may I just stop you there. We'll get to that. I just want to know first if --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: -- you saw the cannon but you did not see it firing; is that right? Whether you heard the later firing, we'll get to that. I just want to know whether you saw the cannon firing. You did not; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I was hiding behind the window and I was watching - of course I was being careful, you know - and I saw that this weapon was going back. This is so loud, is such a loud explosion that it's under your feet and you cannot really mistake it for something else. And then when you see the smoke dispersing -- now was that the moment when I was watching it being fired? Well, really, I cannot say. But I saw the smoke dispersing and then I -- before that the entire building shook.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 16, it should say "smoke."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you know, you know, smoke, dust, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can now have a closer look at the second part of paragraph 9 when you start with the specific -- this specific incident. I just want to summarise the evidence for you and see whether you agree with me or not. Right? So you first heard the alert sirens. Then you heard a very loud explosion that shook the entire building. And then you heard what you assumed it was the sound of a shell falling and then an explosion far away. This is correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, may I just correct you on one thing in this second part. I heard the sound of the trajectory, you know, through the air. And after that, I heard an explosion in the distance. Perhaps there is a bit of difference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were -- you said in your statement that you were inside when this happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, diagnostics, yes. I went to get what we could get as far as medicine was concerned and I was accompanied by the head nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that the alert sirens were activated in case of danger; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what usually happened. They would even -- they would either announce an attack or whatever, but at any rate, yes, they are there as a warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And danger, for example, would be shelling; right ?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And do you also agree with me that when a shell hits a building, the building will shake?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move to a different topic, the -- what you discussed in paragraph 11. You stated that you visited the UN military observers and that you found them in good psychological and physical state, and you also discussed your report here in court today.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So if we could have Exhibit D989.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Dr. Sosic, we also have received already in evidence in this case a report -- the official report that you ordered and signed and you'll have it in front of you in a few moments. This is your report, right? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting and it's not my signature either.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay. I will go then to page 5 in B/C/S. And this is your signature; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And the same with page 3 in B/C/S. And this is also your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So if we now move to page 2 in both English and B/C/S, you can see under number 2, towards the end of the page, you listed some of the hostages and stressed that some of them showed signed of extreme stress.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: You mean this?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, where it says: "Jose Antonio Romero Muelin (Spain) who exhibits signs of extreme stress ..." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we now --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I remember. This is a man who, at the moment when he was taken prisoner and so on, had problems with his wife who was pregnant. So these were the consequences of his inability to communicate with his wife and he was worried, of course, about her pregnancy. But may I say something straight away, please. My friend took his address and the same day upon his return, Dr. Babic called his friends in Spain and they called his wife and said that she shouldn't worry. This was not really in line with military rules, you know, because you know what it's like in the military. However, we looked at all this from a human perspective. So we informed whoever we could and whoever we knew so that they wouldn't worry about their nearest and dearest.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And if we move to the page -- to the following page in B/C/S at the top. Yes, that's right. And you remember -- the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you remember also the case of the other -- that would be page 2 in English, at the end of the page. And do you remember also the other officer from Poland who also exhibits, as you noted, marked symptoms of depression provoked by his uncertain status. Do you remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Mr. Clerieh from the Czech Republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, Janusz Kalbarczyk from Poland. It's at the -- should be at the top of page -- of the page in B/C/S. You can see the name Janusz --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. Yes, Poland, the Polish officer there, yes. Believe me, if that's what I wrote down, that's the way it was. But I cannot recall that he was particularly that way because we made a selection and an analysis and then we said what our priority was in terms of who should be released first, but he didn't seem like that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 4 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And under point 1.1 here, do you remember that another of the things that you noted was that they all complained about the treatment they had received during the first days?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: This pertains to something which I think I wanted to note. The very way in which someone deprives you of your freedom is not pleasant, so this has to do with loss of freedom. That was the first day, because people were completely taken by surprise. They didn't believe that that could happen to them. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: [In English] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And I have just one final issue. At the end of paragraph 5 of your statement you said: "Suffering ..." You have your statement in hard copy in front of you, Dr. Sosic, in a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but which number?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Five, at the end of paragraph 5. So you said in your statement, you said: "Sufferings of Serbian doctors during the war have been described in the movie 'Sarajevo, The Truth Covered by Silence.' I note that some of the events mentioned in this movie have already been described and admitted by the Trial Chamber in the case against Dr. Radovan Karadzic under the Exhibit numbers: D130, D131, D132, D133." And when I asked you at the interview the other day whether you were shown these videos when you reviewed your statement with the Defence, you told me that you were not shown these videos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's what you mean? I said that at this moment I have not seen the movie again. That's in the statement I've given, but I have to confess that it was in 1998. And, you know, human memory is fallible. I could not remember everything. I said I did not see the movie again during the proceedings in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes. And you don't -- in fact, you do not know exactly what these numbers stand for and what the content of these numbers is; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: The numbers relate to that movie. That's all I know, but otherwise they don't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay. And you were not shown the movie now -- you were not shown the movie when you reviewed your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: In The Hague, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That's all I have for this witness. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Iodice. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very brief, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, we'll pick up where you left off with the Prosecutor. Professor, did you know which of your statements the Defence was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew. I am familiar with all the Defence has at its disposal because, in the preparatory procedure, the judge came to see me at Pale, I asked him to see those statements, and I saw the same thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today on page, perhaps, 29, you said you made a triage, a selection, as to setting priorities for captives to be released. Did you make a list?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did that urgently, and I noted, especially concerning this gentleman from Spain, that he should be released urgently and he was, indeed, released two or three days later. And I was so happy that although I'm just a doctor, somebody was willing to listen to me and accept my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that in the document 1D10031, on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I believe I put that on record. I can't see the documents now but it should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that Spaniard? It says also that Jenny Sesita [phoen] talked to her heart's content and cried a lot?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: That's a retired lady, a retired pharmaceutical expert who accompanied us. She wanted to help and she was very emotional in her perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: She was from the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes, she lives somewhere outside of Amsterdam, in a small place, Heerhugowaard, and we actually met a couple of evenings ago, with the leave of the Court, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 27, you were asked if a building would shake when hit by a shell. At the moment you felt the building shake and you saw smoke in connection with that gun, was the building hit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. Those are two different sensations, completely different. It's true I have no experience of being inside a building that is hit, but I can suppose what it feels like, it's completely different. There's this kind of vibration that comes from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the traumatology department ever hit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that it was hit in the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 24, you were asked about the decoration. This is actually an order of compassion. It's an order, not a decoration?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was it that you were awarded this order for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: My contribution in treating the sick and the wounded. I believe also this lady from Holland, this friend of mine, received the same order of mercy. I remember a small celebration was organised and you awarded this. There were other doctors there who received it as well who were prominent doctors who deserved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Ms. Iodice stressed that you received this order from me, as if it were a flaw of the order itself. Do you remember we met during the war at the club of the clinic? Is there anything you could tell the Chamber about me?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SOSIC
utterances.text: I will. If I can take the liberty of saying this, I'm much older than Dr. Karadzic, and at the time when he was a student, I was assistant professor, a lecturer. We were not friends, but at the beginning of the war and during the war I knew him. And what impressed me on the first day, on the 20th August, when I came to Pale after having fled Sarajevo, he was one of the first people who came to greet me and say, "The situation is as it is. We need doctors. There are also other colleagues of yours here. Think about it. People need doctors." But perhaps I had the most contacts with Dr. Karadzic when I needed something. In our co-operation I was not happy with my status, I was not a military doctor. I was a civilian doctor and this relationship did not work very well. And then I would go and see Dr. Karadzic as the president to see if he could do anything to change our status. We had no status. We had no property. We had no families with us, children. And that's when we got the idea to establish a clinical centre that would be a hospital for civilians. Dr. Karadzic welcomed the idea and said he would help us, and that's when a more intensive collaboration began in this spirit of euphoria. We were aware that there's no return for us to Sarajevo and we wanted to create conditions for our patients, our people, our soldiers, that would be decent, not work in a hotel where we pushed out the billiard tables to set up an OR. Dr. Karadzic helped us. I don't know if he used his personal connections, but some architects arrived from Belgrade. I remember this wonderful man, Professor Antic, a very prominent professional who suggested that he make a design for a hospital. And when we started these talks, I realised that Dr. Karadzic, whenever he had a spare moment, would come and see us. It was important to him and we discussed where the hospital could be located, what could be attached to the hospital. And I remember this request that looked unrealistic to me, but one day Dr. Karadzic said, "You know, we should have a theatre here. This is a place where people live." So he took an intensive part in all of this. I believe for him it was some kind of relaxation. And also, as a senior physician, I remember the minister of health asked me to go and see Dr. Karadzic because his knee was injured. The knee was swollen, tender, and warm, and during the examination I asked him how he was taking it and he said, "I have to go and have some recreation, some exercise." utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 1D7947 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document to appear on the screen, Mr. Filipovic, did you hold a rank at the moment when you retired?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they remained in the Army of Republika Srpska until the end of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is everything else then correctly noted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything else is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today in the courtroom as those you were asked while you were being interviewed, would your answers substantially by the same?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Substantially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement based on 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a brief summary of Mr. Zivan Filipovic's statement, a reserve lieutenant-colonel of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I will read it in the English language. [In English] Zivan Filipovic was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bijeljina and later the deputy commander of the 2nd Semberija Brigade. He considers that the inter-ethnic relations between Muslims and Serbs were fine until the mid-1990s. However, when nationalist parties became active and the SDA wished to implement its separatist policies, it disturbed these good relations. Further, staged workers' protests by Muslim employees at the steel plant in Bijeljina in 1990/1991 led to a greater deterioration of good inter-ethnic relations. The steel plant workers used physical violence to capture the factory and plants, also ensuring that the conflict with the police spread through the town. It was well-known that the SDA were responsible for this unrest. When the SDA began being selective in their requests for appointment for important positions throughout the political sphere, it was clear that they had always intended to take control of the municipal, regional, and republican Territorial Defence staffs. This then became the basis for the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. Mr. Zivan Filipovic considers the media stories about the war in Bijeljina and the claims made by Muslims about the activities of the Serbs to be lies by those who actually provoked the fighting in the town. On 30th of March, 1991 [sic], Zivan Filipovic received a call on his home phone reporting shooting in the town centre. He travelled in the direction of the town; however, he was stopped at the barricade which was manned by more than 15 well-armed men. He was told that they were in control of the town and if he did not turn back he would be shot. He recognised some of the men as Muslim citizens and a number of them wore green berets. When Zivan Filipovic returned to the office in April 1992, he saw that the office had been broken into, the files were strewn all over the floor and stairs, and all the weapons that had been assigned to them had been taken by persons unknown. He was informed by colleagues that during the fighting, Muslim citizens had attempted to secure the city through barricades. Muslim snipers were also stationed on the dominant points in Bijeljina and surrounded the hospital and the police station. Further, during the conflict the Muslim forces spread the rumour that Serb soldiers had killed 500 Muslim townspeople who had taken shelter in the military facilities. This rumour had the effect of stirring the Muslims up to the point that they were liable to take up arms again. However, this lie was discovered and the Muslims in Janja surrendered their weapons. In doing so, they demonstrated that they were much better equipped than the Serb soldiers. As a member of the VRS in Brcko, Zivan Filipovic was a witness to almost daily selective artillery -- unselective artillery fire on the centre of the town by artillery and armoured units of the Army of Republic of BH and HVO, frequently using numerous rocket systems. The indiscriminate fire caused major destruction of the civilian facilities and numerous casualties. The Army of Republic of Croatia fired at Brcko too. Zivan Filipovic knew the Geneva Conventions, the international law of war, and humanitarian law, and his soldiers were also familiar with them. No one in his unit violated these. He is aware that members of the Army of BH and HVO did not adhere to these laws, confirmed when an exchange was organised with the Muslim forces and the Serb soldiers were presented with bodies of colleagues who had been captured alive but killed by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you just one question. Before the war you were the deputy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just one correction and I know that it is just the summary read, but the date of the 30th of March, 1991, does not reflect what the witness actually said. He said in his statement the 31st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, as you say in the second paragraph, you say that you were the assistant commander of the Bijeljina municipal Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander and what can you say about him and his activities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1990, the commander was Ljubomir Mitrovic who retired, and by harmonisation concerning the distribution and division of power between the Bijeljina SDA and the SDS, Mr. Saud Abdic was appointed the new commander. He had just graduated and he held the rank of 2nd lieutenant, which was the lowest rank of anyone in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with his view of arming and setting up a paramilitary force and his possible involvement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons of the Territorial Defence staff were held in depots of the JNA barracks in Bijeljina which were secured by the corps of the JNA. We also had some weapons for possible defence that were held in institutions and enterprises where conditions for that had been created, namely, security had to be guaranteed, metal doors, metal safes. As for the plans of defence, that was the part of weapons to be used for an urgent defence of those institutions and enterprises. That was the Territorial Defence plan. Saud Abdic, as the commander, could not have changed them himself even if he wanted to. He was very often absent from work. And in discussions with my other colleagues who were also Muslims, I was told that he went to conduct some training at Kula in Zvornik. The training was the training offered to Bosniaks, future members of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knezevic [sic].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions at this moment for Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First I would again like to thank you for attending an interview with the Prosecution and I will address some of the facts that you told us during the interview as we go. Mr. Filipovic, in paragraphs 7 and 8 of your statement you described how you experienced the start of the fighting on the 31st of March, 1992, and you do not really need to look now at the statement now, only if you need to refresh your memory at some point in time. And we also do not need to go into the details that you have already described in your written statement. But during the interview we had on Monday, you said that it all started when fierce young Muslim men that frequented the cafe Istanbul and fierce young Serbs that frequented the cafe Ravna Gora started fighting with each other. And in this context you also said that the Ravna Gora cafe was frequented by so-called Chetniks associated with Mirko Blagojevic. That's what you told us; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I have a correction to make. I made a technical error. It was the Istanbul cafe and the Srbija cafe. The radically oriented youth used to carry at the Srbija cafe, as you said, and which is correct, and the Bosniak or Muslim youths tended to visit the Istanbul cafe. The cafes are visible one from the other because the distance is between 150 to 200 metres, and it is a fact that the first squaring of accounts took place between these two cafes when a Bosniak, a Muslim, on horseback tried to ride and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Let me interrupt you. We have very little time. I told you this already during our talks on Monday, and therefore if I need more details, I will ask you these details; but otherwise, just be very, very brief in your answers. Mr. Filipovic, there is evidence before this Court --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I refer here to an interview, P02901, that Mirko Blagojevic gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I do not want to show it to you, Mr. Filipovic, but Mr. Blagojevic said that his group threw a grenade into the cafe Istanbul. Could that actually have started the entire affair?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a hand-grenade was thrown at the Istanbul cafe by a young man, and then a horseman set off from the Istanbul cafe to throw a hand-grenade at the Srbija cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, in paragraph 22 of your statement, you refer to the number of casualties that you were aware of and you do not need to repeat this. I make these references only to the statement so that the Judges know where it is actually coming from what I'm saying. And when I asked you during the interview who caused these casualties, you said that these young fierce men that we just spoke about were responsible for this as well as Arkan and his men, Ljubisa Savic, nicknamed Mauzer; the Patriotic League led by Mr. Tiric; and a reconnaissance group of the JNA. And in relation to the reconnaissance group from the JNA, you said that this was a reserve unit comprised of local Serbs commanded by Blagoje Gavrilovic, who later became the commander of the 2nd Semberija Light Brigade of the VRS. You said that, you remember ?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you just changed the sequence a little bit. Members of the Patriotic League were the first to set up barricades and also to position snipers in prominent places, and then there were those who were involved in the Bijeljina war, when they took down the barricades from the facilities and intersections in the Bijeljina town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you told us also on Monday -- or rather, you looked at a small newspaper article from "Slobodna Bosna" --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I refer here to P06185.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and you looked at the names and you remembered an Albanian family and you saw the name in that list from "Slobodna Bosna"; right? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this context can we please have on the screen P02919, page 29. And I hope it works. What is coming up is photos. I want to have page 29, photos that were made at that time. 29. If it is not working, I - it is 29 - I have hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should be e-court page 30 if my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was told it is 29. But 30, yes, try 30. Yes. Can we have this a bit bigger so that Mr. Filipovic can see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, looking at this photo, do you recognise -- do you know these people that are -- one is lying here and the lady is over -- trying to help obviously. Do you know who that is, the lady and the young man?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I see the photographs. I assume that the woman is helping the man, but I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could that be one of this -- one member of the Albanian family that you mentioned that was living near the -- near the barricade where the hospital was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Judging by the face, I don't remember the face at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good. Can we have the next photo -- but before that, look at the clothing that the lady is wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we now have the next photo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that was the last photo. Could you show me the picture again. Yes, this is two pages before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, it's -- according to what we have it's actually ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Filipovic, when you look at this photo now, first of all, do you recognise any of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would that -- looking how they are dressed and the weapons they have, would that be one of your TO men? Would that be the usual TO members? Or can you see from what they are wearing which group they may belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the equipment and the types of weapons there, I assume that they are members of Arkan's unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you look at the bodies that you are finding here and when you look at the location, the surroundings where they are lying, you see that the woman very close to the wall is the one that you saw on the previous photo; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the skirt and sweater, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you look at the location now with this double door, metal door, would that be something you recognise? Could you say what that -- where this location is?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These photos, did you ever see them published during the events in 19 -- in the 1990s? Did you ever see them published? Or is that the first time that you see them here at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on and perhaps also turn -- put this photo off. During your interview on Monday, you said that you were aware that Arkan had established a training centre across the Drina in Badovinci. That's what you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also said that you were not aware that young men from Bijeljina were trained in Badovinci, but you told us that you knew that three men from Bijeljina were trained by Arkan in his training camp in Erdut. And you said that it -- among them was Vojkan Djokovic, Pero Sarov, which is a sort of nickname. But do you now remember who the third person was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the centre in Erdut, a lot before these events in Bijeljina, there were three men, relatively younger men, at the training centre. On which basis? I don't know. One of them was Vojkan Djurkovic, nicknamed Puskar. The other one was Pero and his nickname was Sarov. And the third one was Maletic, nicknamed Promaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Filipovic, you also mentioned when we met on Monday that Arkan had a bad reputation. You consider -- he was considered a criminal and so were his men, and you said that many Serbs were afraid of him and, in fact, all the Muslims. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
