utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, in paragraph 13 of your statement you refer to Arkan and that you do not know how he came to be in Bijeljina. However, we saw here in the court an interview of Mr. Arkan --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that's P02857.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and he himself claims that - and I cite here what he says: "We have come here to help the Serbian population ..." And a sentence further he said: "Therefore we came upon a honourable invitation from the TO of Semberija and Bijeljina from the Crisis Staff to help the Serb people who were in danger there." Mr. Filipovic, you were the TO commander and Arkan refers here to the invitation of the TO Semberija and Bijeljina. Who would that then be if not you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that it's a misquote. It wasn't Semberija and Bijeljina. It's Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have actually -- we can put it on the screen. It's P02857. At least in the English translation that I saw - can we have it on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's ... Yes, in B/C/S it also says "Semberija and Bijeljina" probably but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So at least Arkan says Semberija and Bijeljina. And my question to you was whether you had invited him or, if not you, who else would be TO of Semberija and Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My commander was a Muslim, the commander of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Bijeljina. I was the Chief of Staff, second in command. I've already told you during the interview that he could have been invited by the mentioned three persons, his soldiers, or the radicals who were helping. I claim with full responsibility that no staff of the Territorial Defence or authority of Bijeljina asked Arkan to come and help.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The appearance of Arkan in Badovinci before the conflict broke out, that fuelled the tension in town, did it not? It scared the people and, as you said in particular, all Muslims feared him; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I said - and that's correct - Arkan was a special kind of person. He liked to introduce himself as a hero and liberator. His statements -- well, he made all sorts of statements, full of praise, showing off about his ability to be able to liberate the Serbs. These are not proper official statements within any authority, either in the municipality or the TO staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- quite simply, it's him bragging.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. My question was actually whether his appearance in Badovinci fuelled the tension that was already in the town? That was my question. And that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the stay in Badovinci did not fuel tension or cause anything in town until he entered town actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 40607A on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, while we are waiting for the document, do you know or remember who sent those three young men, including Djurkovic and Maletic, to Arkan's Erdut camp, training camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you would like to hear my opinion, it was Arkan's Volunteer Guard and young men who were vice prone assembled there, tough guys who wanted to be with him and his unit as an important segment of the defence of the Serb people. No one sent them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, back to you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what we are looking here is actually an interview that you gave in 1995 and you may remember that you gave an interview to a group that collected information on the historical events. And what you say here in this document - and you see it here: "Well, the tension and the information about Arkan conducting training in Badovinci and then at the Drina River in Popovic in order to prevent, or rather, to keep under control certain importation of weapons and other material and equipment, this information fuelled the atmosphere even more causing this incident in the night between the 31st of March and the 1st to mark the beginning of the war ..." So at that time when you gave this interview, you did actually say that this contributed, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, stories, as stories go, and stories about Arkan as some kind of dangerous man, were indeed bandied about. Did you hear this or that about Arkan? How come Arkan, and so on and so forth. But his stay did not cause anything massive to happen or did he physically have any impact on Semberija and the town of Bijeljina until the shooting started during the night between the 31st of March and the 1st of April. And then these stories from before about him being dangerous, that he's omnipotent and so on and so forth, that his units were such elite units, I assume, well, that they were reinforced by his entering the area. He was a Fata Morgana for us, Arkan, for Serbs and Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We are very limited in time, sir, and I told you already during the interview that I will interrupt you when it's too detailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P05475 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a report by JNA General Jankovic of 4th April 1992. And, Mr. Filipovic, you knew General Jankovic; right? As a TO commander you would have to co-operate with him; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know General Jankovic personally, but I did know that there was a general with his headquarters in Tuzla, that's the commander of the division, and that he wrote orders for a while to all subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke. I wanted to see P05475 and it should be a report dated 4 April 1992. No, it's again -- it's again the wrong document. Oh, Your Honour, I misspoke. It is P05474, not 75. Yes, yes. That's the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you look at point 2 in the document, General Jankovic refers to: "... the big influence of the SDS and Arkan's propaganda which is felt in the 38th Partisan Division and the 17th Mixed Artillery Regiment because of which some conscripts had left their units with arms." Mr. Filipovic, you as the TO commander, you were aware of these problems; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There were problems. The war that started shocked everyone and everyone became suspicious of everyone else. In my view, it's natural to a degree that things like that would happen, because what is unnatural are the living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you look a bit further down under point 4, General Jankovic states in the second sentence there that: "The town of Bijeljina is controlled by SDS and Arkan's men ..." And he further states that the JNA facilities harbour now 3.000 refugees. So what he says here, that is a picture of how it was; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment upon the figure, whether someone counted the refugees or not, but there were two groups of refugees. They withdrew into barracks. One group was in the Bijeljina barracks and another smaller group of about 500 Muslims took shelter at the Golo Brdo barracks, that's about 3 kilometres from Bijeljina. Now, whether they can be called refugees or not, these were simply people who sought shelter from gun-fire. But there were a number of Serbs among them too. They sought safety in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, when we had the interview on Monday, you mentioned that you met Arkan three times and you told us that first one was in the evening of the 3rd of April, 1992, during a briefing in the JNA barracks which was also attended by Dragan Andjelic, the president of the Executive Board; Milan Novakovic; Novica Simic; and Dragica Makum [phoen]. And you said on this occasion --

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dragisa Masal, commander Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also said that on this occasion, Arkan forcefully requested the hand-over of the barracks to him and his men. That's what you told us; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan wanted to move the training centre from Erdut to Bijeljina, and since the barracks in Bijeljina was very proper, he said that he wanted to throw out the communist officers, the commies as he called them, to take over the barracks and liberate the Serb people from the threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the second time, you told us, was the next day in the municipality building in a meeting with the local authorities during which Arkan again requested the hand-over of the barracks to him and he put great pressure on Zlatko Jokovic. Can you remind me what position Mr. Jokovic had at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokovic at the time was president of the municipality of Bijeljina. When Arkan did not manage to take the barracks from the military, then he tried to have the civilian authorities hand it over to him and he exerted serious pressure on the president of the municipality, and someone informed President Karadzic about what was happening in Bijeljina. So the meeting was interrupted and Zlatko Jokovic returned, perspiring, saying, "I don't know what to do. The president will not allow this to be done. And if I don't do that, Arkan is going to execute me." After a while, as a consequence of that request to hand over the barracks, I think that President Karadzic dismissed the president of the municipality of Bijeljina because of his attempt to co-operate with non-military structures or paramilitary structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Just one other remark. On that same day, there was also Mrs. Plavsic arriving in Bijeljina in a delegation. Were you present also when she arrived or not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The delegation was sent by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and consisted of Biljana Plavsic, Fikret Abdic, and the minister --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The minister of defence -- I wasn't present, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was actually only my question, whether you were present or not. Thank you. During the interview on Monday, you also said that Arkan left on the 6th of April but his Colonel Pejo stayed behind; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From time to time he would stay in Bijeljina, yes, Pejo and a number of other men would be in Bijeljina from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you also mentioned the third time that you met Arkan and you said that was in September 1992, when you were already in the 2nd Semberija Light Brigade of the VRS and deployed at the front line between the Muslim village of Celic and the Serb village of Bobeta Brdo in the Brcko area. And you told us that on this occasion, Arkan and his men came from Lopare municipality and wanted to take revenge for an attack that had occurred against the Serb village of Miroslavci and that he demanded that you and your unit join this attack on Celic. And you also mentioned that he referred to the gold that one could get there during the attack. Does this summarise what you have told us correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He launched an attack on Celic when he came to my unit. The attack was underway. He asked for our support but we had no approval from the superior corps command. But he simply forced us to go into Celic, and on that occasion we pulled out the bodies of three of his dead men and 16 wounded soldiers, and that's where the contact ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have 65 ter 0844 [sic] on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it brings us basically back to Bijeljina in the beginning of April 1992, when you were still in the TO. And as it is coming up it is another report of the 17th Corps of the JNA by General Jankovic of the 7th of April --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it's -- it's again the wrong one. It's again incorrect. Did I misspeak? It's 65 ter 08441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, did you become the commander of the TO at a certain point of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The second in command, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gavrilovic was appointed. I was deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, deputy, I misspoke, Your Honour. I misspoke. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now we have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Under point 2, if you look to point 2, General Jankovic refers again to mobilisation problems and he states that the Bijeljina Crisis Staff would not allow mobilisation. They request that 17th Anti-Artillery Brigade be named Semberska Brigade and that they are to have direct influence on appointments of commanding officer. Do you recall that situation, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think the general is justifying himself a bit here, but it is a fact that the Presidency of the municipality of Bijeljina appointed three men at the beginning of April 1992 because nothing else functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that would be the Crisis Staff, Bijeljina Crisis Staff, or -- because here Mr. Jankovic refers to Bijeljina Crisis Staff. What would he mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I believe the general misspoke, the Presidency of the municipality of Bijeljina appointed Blagoje Gavrilovic, Zivan Filipovic, and Vasilije Andric as the core of the command of the Territorial Defence in the war, but not the Crisis Staff because I would have never been on it. They would have never appointed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- excuse me. I think the witness said he did not belong to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not previously recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I didn't say -- did I call him SDS member?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- probably witness has said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that you have said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware of the time, but I need a bit more time because I needed to address in particular the Arkan section because I'm aware that in other statements, the adjudicated facts in relation to this troop are challenged, and therefore I had to add a few more matters. Therefore, I would need another -- I would think another approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you try to finish before the break, 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will try my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, in paragraph 20 of your statement, you refer to one battalion of the VRS led by Pasaga Halilovic, a Muslim, and you spoke already about it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we need to go briefly into private session, Your Honour, because I wish to address confidential evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, in paragraph 14 of your statement you describe the situation in Janja in April 1992, and you mentioned it also this morning, and how a tragedy could be averted at that time. However, despite this fact, the Muslims from Janja were expelled, were they not, in 1994, to be precise in August/September 1994. You're aware of this; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I know a large number of Muslims from Janja demanded that they re-join their people, but I suppose a number of them were also expelled. Janja was overburdened with Serb refugees from Central Bosnia. It was very, very tense to live there at the time. There was several reasons, some of them wanted to go, and I suppose there was also some coercion, but not from the authorities and not from the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it again this -- this Vojkan that you mentioned? Are you saying he was the one?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Vojkan was prosecuted for these actions. There was a trial. Muslim witnesses were heard and the proceedings were interrupted. In fact, Vojkan Djurkovic was acquitted of the charges that he had forcibly expelled Muslims. That was a -- the judgement of the court in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My last topic with you, Mr. Filipovic, is what you told us about on Monday, that on the 3rd of May, 1992, Mauzer on the public square in Bijeljina with a megaphone called on the people to set off to liberate Brcko, and you said that 12 buses indeed departed to Brcko, including Mauzer's men, Gavrilo's men, TO and MUP troops. And my question to you is: You yourself did not go on that -- at that time or did you also join?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. That convoy set off on the 3rd of May at the invitation of the people from Brcko to help liberate the hospital, the health centre which was on fire, and the road. I went to Brcko on a mission on the 6th of May, three days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have P02889 on the screen, and it should be -- I hope this time it's the right one. It should be a report, an extraordinary report, of 29 September 1992 by Captain Cutoric from the Eastern Bosnia Corps command in which he describes the activities in Brcko - and it's to the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you look at the first bigger paragraph he says or writes, rather: "The town was flooded by different 'patriotic' oriented individuals who used 'devotion to Serbism' as an excuse for robbery, rapes, and as a result of that, murders for no justified reasons." And two lines further down he says: "We also believe that there were groups which came as ordered, that is, who had the support of the then military and civilian authorities. And here we mean the leadership in Bijeljina, which in fact brought 550 gathered 'fighters' at the very beginning of the war. The most notorious of all were Mauzer and Major Gavrilovic with Arkan's men led by Peja and the civilian authorities in Bijeljina." Mr. Filipovic, your corps command, because you belonged to this corps, describes the activities of the troops from Bijeljina here; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that the Brcko theatre was very iffy, that in addition to the regular units of the army and the MUP, certain small groups raided Brcko and of their own accord created rather big problems and hurt the reputation of both the MUP and the army. We did not have enough forces to secure the town of Brcko and protect it from these violent groups that came from I don't know where and then left I don't know where. One of such groups was the Obilic men from Kosovo. Another was the group of Zika the Montenegrin. Self-organised groups who came as volunteers to help the Serbs, but in fact they came to loot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: One last document, Mr. Filipovic, I want to show you and that is P02855, and it should be coming up now here, a report of the 1st Krajina Corps command to the VRS Main Staff dated 13 -- it should be something 13 August 1992. It's the wrong ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, no, it's correct. It's 28th -- it's correct, yes. It's the 28th July 1992. And it is from Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. And if you look at the first -- very first paragraph he refers here to the various groups like Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Captain Dragan, and so on and so forth. And he lists then in the next paragraph their main characteristics and he refers to them to have low moral quality. A bit further down he says that many formations of this type display hatred of non-Serb peoples, and I quote: "One can conclude without reservation that they are -- that that are the genocidal elements among the Serbian people." And in the next line he refers to looting. Mr. Filipovic, that is a fair description of the behaviour of such troops that Mr. Tolimir here states; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: These things happened. And these false pretenses of patriotism, et cetera, that's true. Those groups were bent on looting. Honourable people honestly reported to military units if they wished to serve. In addition to the military police we have the police force and the MUP. There were so many such pests that we could not protect or defend the population. The 2nd Semberija Brigade held for four months a military police company in Janja and they barely managed to protect the population of Janja from looting and robbery at the beginning of the war. I don't know how else to explain it, but I suppose dogs of war turn up in every war, bent on profiteering and all types of vice, least of all to help their own people, Muslim, Serb, or any other people. They are simply members of paramilitary groups, groups of robbers and looters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, let's look now at page 5 in both languages, please. And as you can see here that Colonel Tolimir refers to -- it's in the middle, it's in the middle of the page in both languages. He refers to Bijeljina, and I quote again: "The Serbian National Guard in Bijeljina has formally joined the so-called special brigade. The Serbian National Guard was formed by the Bijeljina SDS, and the Presidency of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly decided that this would be the army of Bijeljina which would defend Bijeljina should it be attacked and appointed self-styled Major Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, as the commander." And he said: "The greater part of the municipality authorities in Bijeljina still back that Guard." Mr. Filipovic, that's again Mr. Tolimir assessing now Mauzer's men, and he's right in this, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tolimir was a security organ and Mauzer and the Guard were part of the 3rd Corps. There was no love lost between them, but the corps was superior to the Bijeljina Brigade. There were certain misunderstandings, I suppose, definitely, and other minor things, but they were subordinated to the military command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when we spoke on Monday, you mentioned that Mauzer was early on seen around the office of the SDS. So what Colonel Tolimir says, that it was formed by the Bijeljina SDS, that would be correct; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb National Guard was set up by Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, to be on a par with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, to have his own guard just like Arkan did. So that Arkan's guard would leave and the other would stay behind to keep Bijeljina. Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, tried with his strict attitude and harsh discipline to imitate Arkan's guard and hold himself out as the only protector and defender of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Filipovic, this special brigade, the Serbian National Guard, would also escort Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik when they came to Bijeljina or passed through to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I just had -- was of the impression if the parties could come up with some agreed facts, for example, on paramilitaries, some questions could have been dispensed with. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder session of today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could introduce to you and the Chamber Zygimantas Juska, who is one of our interns from Lithuania and joining us this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much, Your Excellencies, but it is necessary, though, to clarify some issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you talk about the lack of love which existed between the civilian and military structures, can you tell us approximately what the basis for that was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think that alongside the war that was waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was also a civilian war, and that the newly elected authorities were as a rule anti-communist people and the officers from the former JNA, the former Yugoslavia, were mostly communists and there was a degree of distrust between the ideology of the former communist system and the new system with ethnic-based political parties and the new understanding of matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that that was the basis for the lack of trust. Whether the communists would support the ethnic groups, one or the other or some other peoples, it was believed that the communists were people with a tendency to act differently in similar situations. That was the substance, in my view, of this distrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have P02855, that is to say, show it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will try to read out to you something from the document as the font is quite small. "Not one of the paramilitary formations expressed its affiliation to the ruling political party, the SDS. Quite the contrary, all of them have the political markings of the opposition parties from Serbia, SPO, SNS ..." and so on and so forth. How does this information and the assessment of the then-Colonel Tolimir fit with your knowledge of the party membership of those paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the military security had special ways of monitoring and assessing the conduct of groups and military units and organs, and in reports these assessments are often expressed. Paramilitary formations, mostly from Serbia - I mentioned one of them from Kosovo - did not arrive influenced by any ideology, either the communist ideology or any other. I believe that they came to "help" the Serbs but they were actually coming to achieve gain and to loot. That was why the military leadership - I specifically mean the 3rd Corps command and the municipal authorities, and in particular I would stress the leadership of the state, I mean your role and the role of General Mladic, to shake off these paramilitary formations which only caused damage, both to the people and the army and the political sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do not need this document anymore. On page 62 of today's transcript you were asked about expulsions from Janja and about Vojkan. And you said that Vojkan was released and that Muslims testified at his trial, the Muslims from Bijeljina. I did not understand whether those from Janja testified as well. Could you tell us how these witnesses, Muslims whom he was taking to the other part of the country, testified at the trial?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They testified on behalf of Vojkan Djurkovic, aka Puskar, because they believed that he was helping them in difficult conditions to go out into the territory under the control of Bosnian Muslims and that it would be much easier for them there. The substance of their request to leave Janja was not any sort of political pressure except for a huge number of Serbs who had arrived to the populated place called Janja. I have the information that from 28 municipalities of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina there were Serbs who arrived to Janja. So there was a mixture of various customs, habits, ways of life, and everything else. Around 10.000 refugees in Janja and 10.000 locals in a small space in very difficult living conditions without sufficient food, water, without sufficient living space and so on and so forth, all made the living conditions there insupportable. For the same reason, I have the information, and I believe that it is true, that a lawyer from Tuzla would submit to Vojkan, he was a Bosniak, a Muslim, Pasic, he would submit to Vojkan the lists of people who were to be taken to the regular places for exchange which were made possible by the army. They should be brought there so that they would be exchanged; that is to say, they would be handed over to Tuzla and they would join their compatriots. And I believe that the bulk of the witnesses who testified on behalf of Vojkan were from the place of Janja, and after he was released he boasted around Janja that he had not done anything and that the Muslims had testified and said that he was actually helping them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Mr. Pasaga Halilovic and those several among the 50 or so who were included but did not wish to leave?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the details. I know certainly that Pasaga Halilovic was at the head of a battalion of the Muslim army which was fighting as part of the Eastern Bosnia Corps of the 3rd Semberija Brigade in the Posavina area, that they were loyal. That is to say, they responded to the call-ups without any forms, they set up a unit and the reserve officer, reserve major, he was at the head of this unit. And the municipal leadership and the commanding officers from the corps were horrified and it wasn't clear to anyone -- let me not say that they regretted why that happened. And the method which was used to take them there is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if they were returned and where Mr. Halilovic is living now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he is living at the moment but I know that one of his brothers who used to be a teacher at the agricultural school and who was also a member of this unit is still living in Bijeljina. And as for Pasaga, I think that he's somewhere in the Federation. He was an official in the Bijeljina municipality. He was also a director of some enterprises and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who replaced Mr. Pasaga Halilovic in the position of this battalion's commander?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When both for Serbs and for Muslims -- I'm not sure about Muslims, but for Serbs it was an untoward event. It was something -- let me not say unheard of or not normal for the Serbs. Mujica Jahic was appointed to his position. In that period he used to be the director of the waterworks and sewage in Bijeljina, he was also a reserve officer and he replaced Mujica Jahic in that position and he led this unit to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I could guess his ethnicity, but other participants in the trial cannot judge by the names. Can you tell us what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mujica was a Muslim. He's now a Bosniak, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also shown several documents signed by General Jankovic. Where was General Jankovic's seat or headquarters, rather, at the time when he made the assessments of the events in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General Jankovic was the commander with his headquarters in Tuzla, and all the events in Bijeljina and the surrounding area as well as the attempt to move the Tuzla garrison with the management of General Jankovic and the events at Brcanska Malta, let me not talk more about that, were the cause for him to issue certain orders. Such as, for example, to mobilise the Territorial Defence unit and secure the left bank of the Drina, which was absurd. Or, for example, I cannot judge what were the channels through which General Jankovic obtained this information, probably through the security and intelligence organs. However, it seems to me that they also ascertained the situation somewhat one-sidedly and then they reported to their superior so that General Jankovic did not have - and I claim this with full responsibility - he did not have 100 per cent truthful information from the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you know, did the SDS take part in combat that took place in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS as a political party certainly did not get involved militarily. However, the seat of the Municipal Board of Bijeljina was used during the civilian war as a gathering place for the army and so on. The SDS members did go out to the front, but not as a unit, a political unit or a political body, but as members of military unit. So, Mr. President, I have to -- their political affiliation was one thing and their military engagement was something completely different. There was no political unit and only political unit in the territory of the Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. I have no further questions. Thank you for coming here to testify, and thank you for being a proper official of Republika Srpska even though you were not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ZIVAN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Filipovic. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as the Trial Chamber and thank you to ICTY which will investigate everything and determine justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasojevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. I take it you hear me in the language you understand, Mr. Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Spasojevic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to make pauses between what I say and what you say, that is to say, between question and answer, and also to speak unhurriedly so that everything would be recorded. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D7946 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see in front of you a statement which you have given?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask that the last page be shown to the witness now so that the signature would be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully convey what you said and the information you expressed and is there anything that should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything is well recorded and well conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today as you were asked at the time when you gave the statement, would your answers substantially be the same?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this statement. And one document mentioned in paragraph 15 is something that I will lead live as it has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson, as regards the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Mr. Dusan Spasojevic in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry for translation. My apologies to interpreters. Dusan Spasojevic was born on 23rd of October, 1958, in Bijeljina, and currently resides in the village of Dazdarevo. He was an inspector of the crime police at the SJB Bijeljina. Dusan Spasojevic and his colleagues obtained intelligence information that clearly indicated growing ethnic divisions between the Serbs and the Muslims in Bijeljina. While Serbs wishing to preserve the political status quo were assigned to the regular forces of the country, Muslims joined paramilitary units in Croatia and took part in terrorist operations against the JNA. Between 1990 and 1992, the SDA, Muslim party, which had full control over the Ministry of the Interior of BH, used its resources to select Muslim members of the reserve police force and send them to Croatia for training. Hasan Tiric, for example, was a member of the SDA Main Board in Bijeljina and was secretly arming Muslims and making preparations to carry out terrorist acts. Maps made by Muslim extremists showing Serbian houses marked with crosses indicate clearly the nature of the conflict that unfolded in Bijeljina. As early as late 1990, there were almost daily reports of harassment and abuse committed against Serbian women by young Muslim men at the town's markets. In the same period, another group of young Muslims stormed Serbian catering facilities, causing ethnically motived fights. Dusan Spasojevic and his colleagues concluded that these groups were organised and committed to instigating ethnic divisions and creating disorder. By mid-1991, the situation was so severe that the Bijeljina Muslims only visited restaurants and bars owned by Muslims, while the Serbs visited those owned by Serbs. Meanwhile, the local authorities of the municipality, the JNA garrison, and the police were working with all their powers to calm tensions and improve inter-ethnic relations. On 30th of March, 1992, a Serb detonated an explosive device at a restaurant. The perpetrator was apprehended by the on-site investigation team, led by a Serb. This incident demonstrates that the police and local authorities were resolved to calm the situation and bring law breakers to justice, including where the perpetrators of crimes were Serbs too. Around 27th of March, Dusan Spasojevic was informed of an explosion in the premises of the SDA. Upon attending the scene, he found some 20 to 30 Muslims gathering -- gathered who behaved threateningly and prevented Spasojevic and his official colleagues from entering the premises. Intelligence later revealed that weapons were soon transferred from the SDA premises to a nearby mosque. Dusan Spasojevic believes that he was prevented from accessing SDA premises after the explosion in order to hide the stockpiling of weapons there. On the 1st of April, 1992, Dusan Spasojevic discovered a roadblock near his premises operated by 15 well-armed men. These men later opened fire without warning on a marked police vehicle as well as nearby onlookers which included a number of children. Dusan Spasojevic's residence was known as a building housing police officers and their families. He observed more roadblocks in neighbouring streets and believes that these were set up deliberately to prevent policemen from calming disorder in the town. Later that day, those arming the roadblocks started shooting at soldiers, ordering the blocks be dismantled. Dusan Spasojevic was informed by the duty officer at the police station that all major roads and intersections were blocked by armed Muslims and the local hospital was completely encircled. On high buildings of the town snipers were observed randomly opening fire. During the day many Serbs fled the town to nearby villages. Dusan Spasojevic believes the evidence shows that these events were planned in advance by Bijeljina's armed Muslims. Mr. Dusan Spasojevic was never ordered by anybody to do anything to the detriment of the non-Serb citizens and he never gave such an order to his subordinates. The actions of Dusan Spasojevic and his subordinates were in line with the law and focused on the well being of all citizens regardless of their ethnic background. All crimes against non-Serbian citizens were properly investigated and, where possible, perpetrators were handed to the relevant authorities. Dusan Spasojevic was also involved in the commission investigating the events surrounding Srebrenica 1995. This commission concluded that the Muslim side in Bosnia falsely claimed that 8.000 Muslims were killed there by claiming Muslim soldiers who were killed in the breakthrough and in previous clashes of the war were innocent victims in Srebrenica. A report presenting these facts was submitted but rejected by the republican MUP under the pressure of international representatives. And that would be short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about paragraph 2. It says that from 1997 until 2006, for ten years, you were commander of the police station in Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I had been police commander for about three years but then I also did other work in the crime police, but I was in the service non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it necessary for the international police force to certify you and were you certified as eligible for police work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in your statement Mr. Tiric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D15018 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, can you tell us what you know about the units that were later commanded by Mr. Tiric?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tiric Hasica was a criminal before the war and, perhaps in 1989, I filed a regular criminal report against him for aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: This report was filed by my colleagues, that is to say, they interviewed Tiric Hasica, or rather, persons who were at the barricades. And after the armed conflict, they voluntarily handed over their weapons to the Bijeljina public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I just note that we did receive a translation of this document this morning. It's not yet uploaded in e-court, but we have it in Sanction now in both languages if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Article this is, 151?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure, and on that basis, a criminal report is filed with the office of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say something about the rest? Did you know any of these other people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew most of these other people, some by sight, some I know better. Quite a few of them are criminals, among them Hasica Tiric as one of the most prominent ones, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English. It says "Tiric Hasan" and then come the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, why were criminal reports filed against them here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was armed rebellion, I think, according to the law that was then in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Hasan Tiric participate in the events of the 31st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, since my police building was surrounded by five or six roadblocks, I noticed him. He had a vehicle, a Ford, with a Zvornik licence plate and I saw him going from one roadblock to another. Also he used a fire truck and a small TAM truck. I saw him a few times in the morning hours while I was in my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that that is a building where policemen lived. Was there a difference in terms of the places where the barricades were, in terms of where buildings were and where particular neighbourhoods were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire building was blocked, it was a residential building, and all of the exits and entries were blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We note that this criminal report is essentially a summary of information, and based on the list of attachments at the end of the report, although none of the attachments are included, it appears that this document is largely based on the contents of third-party statements. So it does raise some of the concerns the Chamber has raised previously about such statements, concerns that are amplified by the fact that since we don't have those attachments or statements, we can't assess how accurately this report summarises them. And on top of that, the statements appear to be war-time statements taken by the Bosnian Serb police of ethnic Muslims, and in light of the pattern of abuse by Bosnian Serb police forces of ethnic Muslims in this case and I would refer to adjudicated facts 863, 937, 1327, 2288, 2437, 2536, and 2652 as examples, this raises further reliability concerns. However, I believe I -- I believe some of the assertions in this document bear on assertions the witness has made in his statement and I will be using this document to test some of those assertions. So in the circumstances, I'm not going to object to the admission of the document. I just note these reliability concerns in terms of the weight that it should ultimately be given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for Mr. Spasojevic at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The adjudicated facts you referred to were mainly related to general circumstances where Muslim people were detained, not specifically for the purpose of criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Some of them involved interrogations, but not necessarily -- they weren't all necessarily detention for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Spasojevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted in most part in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to stay on this criminal report for a moment so if we could go back to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The subjects of this criminal report, Mr. Spasojevic, the report against Hasan Tiric and others, they're all Muslims including 28 Muslims who the report acknowledges at the time were dead; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You don't know? The report makes it clear --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You don't know whether they're all ethnic Muslims or you don't know whether 28 of them were dead at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: All of them are ethnic Muslims, but I don't know whether there were that many dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 39 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Here the report says that the reported persons listed under the numbers 133 to 160, and then it names a number of people, after the breakout of armed conflicts, et cetera, were actively engaged as Muslim and Albanian extremists at the barricade set up in JNA street near the hospital where they lost their lives. So reported persons listed under numbers 133 to 160 of this report were dead at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was not working on that case and I did not review those corpses, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could go to page 51 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S. And in the beginning of the first full paragraph in the English and at the top of the page in the B/C/S, it talks about the -- on the third day of the armed conflicts in Bijeljina, so this would be the 3rd of April, the Muslim fanatics exulting at having easily have taken the town tried to intimidate the Serbs as much as possible. And then in the next paragraph it says during the third and fourth days of the conflict, which would be the 3rd and 4th of April, the self-organised people of Semberija managed to remove some of the barricades in the town and rout the Muslim extremists from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this description of events on the 3rd and 4th of April, Mr. Spasojevic, is almost entirely false. The Muslims never took the town, let alone easily. It was not the self-organised people of Semberija who removed the barricades, but principally Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guard paramilitary force, which I note is not mentioned anywhere in this report. And furthermore, Arkan's men started removing those barricades immediately, and by the 3rd of April, it was Arkan, not the Muslims, who controlled the town; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let's go to P2629. And if we could go to the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S and the top of page -- I'm sorry, bottom of page 1 in the English, top of page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see this says that: "The security situation in Bijeljina was disrupted on 31st March 1992 at about 2030 hours in the evening when barricades were set up in the centre of the town by Muslim extremists. During the night and the next day the Territorial Defence" - if we go to the next page in the English - "the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard started removing the barricades under the supervision of the Bijeljina SO Crisis Staff." So it's clear from this police report that the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard, otherwise known as Arkan's men, started removing the barricades right away, during the night of the 31st of March and morning of the 1st of April; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The roadblocks were removed only around 10.00 or 11.00 on the following day, because I watched the removal of one barricade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. In line 12 the witness said the removal started at 10.00, not that it ended then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you say "the following day," do you mean the 1st of April or the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The date? I cannot focus now, but the barricades were there all night. So the day after that first day, between 10.00 and 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you only saw one barricade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw the removal of one barricade, but from my building, from the roof of the building where I live, I saw four barricades -- five.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to D1612 now. And if we could go to page 11 in both languages. And if could direct your attention towards the top of the page in the B/C/S, towards the middle of the page in the English. This is an interview that Arkan gave after the events about what happened in Bijeljina. And he states that: "We arrived in the course of the night ..." And a few lines down he says: "It was night; however, we entered Bijeljina as a unit and we took the centre." It says: "The fighting was merciless ..." And towards -- about eight or nine lines down he says: "Naturally, we had military experience. We came with big battles behind us and we entered as a military ... as a unit and we took Bijeljina fast." And if we go to the next page, towards the middle in the English, towards the top third in the B/C/S, he's asked: "Who was the real boss in Bijeljina at the time?" And he says: "Well, I was the real boss of Bijeljina at the time. But at our check-points, for example, that Dogo," and then he's corrected and says "Doko." And then he starts to tell a story about how Bojan Curkovic [phoen] was holding a check-point. "Doko, Abdic and Simovic came along and they were forced to lie down on the ground." Then he says: "They were sent back that evening, but we agreed they would come back the next day." And then he describes how they came back the next day with Mrs. Plavsic. So it's clear that this event at the check-point would have been the 3rd of April because the delegation, we know, came on the 4th. So that indicates that Arkan had set up check-points and was controlling who entered the town on the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So these documents, Mr. Spasojevic, make clear that the description of the conflict in the criminal report against Hasan Tiric falsely represents the Muslims as the dominant military force and falsely claims that the Serbs were a local self-organised force even though Arkan's involvement was common knowledge. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one explanation, please. How come this interview is an official document and an official criminal report is not? This should be called interview rather than document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's a very inappropriate and unacceptable intervention. You may take up that issue in your re-examination. Yes, please continue -- do you remember the question, Mr. Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not correct. Arkan enjoyed promoting himself and bragging in the media. I have information to the effect that there were about 15 or 16 of them there. There was this clash with the guests, but he did not set up roadblocks. There weren't any check-points of his anywhere as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to P5474, an official document. And if we could look at point 4, towards the bottom of the page, this is a report from the 17th Corps of the JNA dated the 4th of April. And under number 4 it says: "The situation in the territory is extremely complex. The town of Bijeljina is controlled by the SDS and Arkan's men who do not even allow our armoured unit to each certain positions in the town."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Spasojevic, whether or not Arkan had any check-points or not, he was able to control even whether the JNA entered the town, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I see this is a report from some military command. I'm a policeman and that's why I wouldn't like to go into this, but I know there were no check-points and Arkan could not control entry and exit into the town. I'm a local and I went all over town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So one last question about Arkan. Because you also give a very detailed about events in early April in your statement and you don't mention Arkan at all. Did you not think Arkan's involvement in the conflict in Bijeljina was sufficiently important to even mention it in your sworn evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: He's absolutely inconsequential to me because I had had some problems with his men concerning crime and I saw no reason to mention him specially.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you about the people who were killed in the conflict. You didn't see anyone actually -- you didn't personally witness anyone getting killed in the conflict in early April, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement at paragraph 20 you said that after the initial conflict, dead bodies were picked up by a utility vehicle, accompanied by the police, and placed in the morgue. Did you personally participate in this process of collecting the bodies or is this just something you learned about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see any of these dead bodies before they were collected, lying in the streets or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think when with my family and my children I was going towards the village, I saw one corpse in Majevicka Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And apart from this one corpse, did you see any others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And these bodies were simply collected from the streets. There were no on-site investigations conducted; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I note also that the criminal report against Hasan Tiric also states that a number of persons including Redzep Sabanovic lost their lives at or around the barricade near the hospital. And that's at pages 51 and 52 of the English. Do you recognise this location, the location in this photo, as being a location near the Bijeljina hospital, near where the barricade was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The photograph -- perhaps. I cannot really judge. I'm really sorry. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the criminal report back in Sanction and go to page 51 and 52 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S. And this is towards the bottom of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the passage that talks about the Muslims who were killed around the barricade at the hospital, and it asserts: "During the crushing of the barricade near the hospital, the following persons lost their lives at or around the barricade while they were putting up armed resistance ..." And then it lists a number of persons. And there's no source identified so I'd like to ask you, Mr. Spasojevic, what is the specific source of this information that these Muslims were putting up armed resistance when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know Redzep Sabanovic by any chance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know his -- that his wife -- Aisa Sabanovic, was that his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you confirm that Aisa Sabanovic is a Muslim female name; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The list of attachments to this report includes a number of death certificates related to the report and it includes Aisa Sabanovic's death certificate in that list. But the report doesn't say anywhere anything about how Aisa Sabanovic was killed. Do you know why the report didn't say anything about the cause of her death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And this passage of the report also includes Bego Sindric as someone who was killed at or around this barricade and whose body was collected on the 5th or 6th of April. But another witness in this case, a Defence witness, Dr. Kicanovic testified that Bego Sindric was wounded in the conflict and in fact he died in hospital a few days later. And that's transcript page 34891. Are you able to reconcile that inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Spasojevic, at paragraph 20 of your statement you said that approximately half of the victims of the conflict in early April were killed during street fighting. But it's clear from your evidence that you didn't see any of the bodies except for one, you didn't see anyone actually getting killed, you don't know anything about their injuries, there were no on-site investigations, and I've just asked you about the source of information in this report about how these people were killed and the basis for the assertion that they were killed putting up armed resistance, and you had no idea. So basically you're just guessing when you say that half the victims were killed during street fighting. You really have no idea; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do know, after all there is talk among colleagues, we are all policemen, and from these conversations with colleagues I came to that conclusion. This is not a precise conclusion when I said that half of them died in street fighting. It's not precise. It's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd just like to ask you one last question about this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 59 of the English and page 24 in the B/C/S which is the list of attachments. And if we could go to the next page -- if you just scan your eyes down this list of attachments and if we could go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There are a total of 65 listed attachments, mostly written statements and death certificates. But in your statement you said that in the attachment to this criminal report there was a fax sent from the Tuzla SDA to the Brcko SDA regarding the dispatch of armed combatants to Bijeljina to fight the Serbs in Bijeljina. But that document isn't listed anywhere in this list of attachments, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: That fax circulated beginning with 1992 because the premises of the SDA in Njegoseva Street were demolished. I believe that fax was found on the premises of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation for the fact that it's not listed in these attachments even though you assert that it was attached to this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: It should be, as a rule, attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 18 of your statement you asserted that all crimes against the non-Serbian citizens in Bijeljina municipality were handled by the members of the public security station in Bijeljina, and any possible perpetrators that were uncovered were handed over to the relevant prosecution offices. And later in your statement at paragraph 25 you discuss the September 1992 murder of members of two families, the Sarajlic and Mujagic families, a crime that you state was condemned by the whole community. Now, it's correct, is it not, that members of these families were taken out of their homes and executed on the banks of the Drina River near the village of Balatun and that Dusko Malovic's special police unit was widely suspected of perpetrating that crime; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 25 of your statement you said you gave a statement about this incident a couple of years ago, three years ago, and that this crime is still pending. Now, the reason it's still pending, Mr. Spasojevic, is that no investigation into this crime was initiated until 2002, when the Bijeljina prosecutor's office requested the Bijeljina police to look into this incident; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 24768.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also if Mr. Reid could send us that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from the Bijeljina public security centre to the regional office of the prosecutor in Bijeljina about this case. And the title is your request from 26 February 2002 to collect intelligence. And it says: "Pursuant to your request ... we have checked the operational files in the CJB Bijeljina, police station Bijeljina, and those of the former reserve police station in Brodac, and we have established that there is no written trace in relation to the crime described in your request and that our organ did not submit the criminal report to the competent office of the prosecutor." And that's a confirmation of the fact that this crime was not investigated at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now to 65 ter 24773.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an official note of the Bijeljina police station of the 3rd of June, 2002, again it's in relation to this investigation into this crime and it's an official note of an interview with Momcilo Djilas. And as you can see, Mr. Djilas told the Bijeljina police that in 1992 he was a member of the reserve police station in Brodac. And about five lines down the first paragraph he says that the commander of the police station Radoljub Ivanovic ordered him, Milo Skoric and Miodrag Tomic to go to the ferry in Balatun and take bodies of people who had been killed the night before who are presently at the bank of the Drina River and throw them in the Drina River. Another five or six lines down he describes the scene. He says "when I came close to the water bed" he could -- he said he could see bodies of people he recognised in the water, Izo Sarajlic, Osman Sarajlic and his daughter, as well as Osman Sarajlic's wife, and the body of their 10 to 12-year-old daughter and as others. And if we go to the next page in the English, he says: "Since the bodies were in the water and since there were no bodies at the coast," I think he means the river-bank, "we had no need to throw them into the water. We returned from the site where we informed the commander Ivanovic that somebody had already thrown the bodies into the water before us and that we covered the body and splattered brains with earth so as not to get the flies and wasps on it. Upon hearing that, the commander said, 'You did well.'" Now, the note was taken by Borislav Ivanic and Milenko Djokic, are these police officers that you worked with at the Bijeljina police station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you say that they were professionals and you can rely on the accuracy of their official note?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: You can rely on its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you know this former reserve police station officer who was interviewed, Momcilo Djilas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And he was in 1992 a member of the Brodac reserve police station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know that independently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but I've read it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you know that the commander of the reserve police station was Radoljub Ivanovic, was that something you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, based on your own information, that this location where the bodies were found that Mr. Djilas describes, the banks of the Drina River and in the Drina River near Balatun, is that consistent with your information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I did not have this information, in 1992. And later on, I was involved in gathering some notes and documents that were later forwarded to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is this information consistent with the other information you gathered?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you gather any other information about members of the police, specifically the Brodac reserve police station, being involved in concealing the remains of these victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: All the documentation that was gathered was forwarded to the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. I cannot remember any longer all that we managed to gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 24816.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is another document from this investigation that was commenced in 2002 and it is a certificate issued by the RS Red Cross at the request of the Bijeljina MUP and judicial organs, listing a number of missing persons from these families. And if you could just scan down this list and indicate whether this list of missing persons is consistent with your information about the victims, the identity of the victims of this crime.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one last question about this incident, Mr. Spasojevic. As you were involved in this investigation that was initiated in 2002, did the information that was gathered in the course of that investigation, in light of that information did Dusko Malovic's special police unit remain the prime suspects in the case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just about to move to another topic and it will start with a somewhat lengthy document, so if the Court wishes to adjourn now, it would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do so. But before we do so, Mr. Robinson, are we going to hear Mr. Vucurevic tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we're not able to do that. We tried, actually, but the security is unable to accommodate a proofing at a time when it would have been possible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having looked at his statement very briefly, the Chamber has found that while there are parts which are relevant and important, but some part also pertains to the Nevesinje area which is in Herzegovina and not in the indictment. So when preparing the revised statement could you take a look into the matter and a substantive part -- majority of the associated exhibits seem to have been related to that area. Mr. Spasojevic, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow at 9.00. In the meantime I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.43 p.m.,
